extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, educational theorists, teachers, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and evaluative criteria for designing and judging general and vocational education (freedom, individuality, methods, and vocational training through occupations) as argued in a chapter on vocational aspects of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom as an intellectual attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom designates a mental attitude rather than external unconstraint of movements; it means intellectual initiative, independence in observation, judicious invention, foresight of consequences, and ingenuity of adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom should be fostered by conditions that enable thinking: genuine questions that instigate curiosity, equipment permitting interests to take effect, and situations where pupils' own purposes direct actions. Anti-patterns: equating freedom with mere physical unconstraint or passive absence of social guidance; tolerating docility, memorization, and intellectual servility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning as social and active
rubrics_metrics.description: When learning is a phase of active undertakings involving mutual exchange, social control enters into the very process of learning; absence of the social factor makes learning a purely individual carry-over with no reason to give socialized direction to dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design learning tasks that require cooperation, mutual exchange, and shared aims so that social direction is inherent in the learning activity. Avoid isolating instruction from methods of school government and from group activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of instruction and school government
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often a separation between method of instruction and methods of government; the school should avoid this antithesis and create a social atmosphere and motive for learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that pedagogical methods and school governance reinforce the same social aims (e.g., responsibility, participation). Anti-pattern: strong external discipline in government combined with rote, individualistic instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for individuality and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuality means (1) doing one's own thinking and (2) natural variations in point of view, appeal of objects, and mode of attack; suppressing these variations in the interest of uniformity causes confusion, artificiality, and destroys originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow different modes of approach, encourage pupils' own problems and purposes, and avoid forcing all learners into a single mold of study and recitation. Example: value unexpected student reactions as legitimate educational material rather than irrelevant deviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as unforced response (not product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality in education is unforced response of one's individuality, not originality measured by product; learners should experience genuine discovery from their standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate and design tasks that allow learners to discover and reformulate subject matter themselves. Do not judge student originality only by professional-level products; recognize developmental standpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of physical experimentation and self-activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-activity in education must include free use of sensory and motor organs: investigation, experimentation, trying out ideas on materials and appliances; enforced physical quietude may be unfavorable to realizing problems and testing ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide opportunities for hands-on exploration and experimentation, especially for learners who are still finding their intellectual way. Anti-pattern: restricting physical activity under the mistaken notion that mental freedom equals stillness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom requires leeway of movements as well as mental initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: The freedom involved in teaching and studying is identified with the thinking that enlarges and refines what a person already knows; this quality of mind cannot develop without a fair leeway of movements in exploration, experimentation, application, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance opportunities for concentrated, quiet study with periods of active exploration; structure environments so intellectual initiative is supported by appropriate physical and material freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocation defined as significant, continuous activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A vocation means such a direction of life activities as renders them perceptibly significant to a person and useful to his associates; occupation is a concrete term for continuity and includes artistic capacity, scientific ability, effective citizenship, and professional, business, or mechanical labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame curricular aims so vocation is understood broadly (not limited to manual trades) and as continuous purposeful activity rather than a narrowly technical job description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject educating for one exclusive specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Vocations are not to be distributed in an exclusive way; each individual has a variety of callings and nothing is gained by educating a person for only one line of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs that develop multiple capacities and avoid over-specialization. Anti-pattern: predetermining a single, irreversible vocational track for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency of a vocation depends on its association with other callings
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's efficiency in a specialized calling is determined by its association with other callings; exclusive dominance of a vocation tends to emphasize technical skill at the expense of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate cross-disciplinary and civic/relational learning into vocational preparation so that specialized skills are informed by broader life experiences and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation organizes knowledge and supports learning
rubrics_metrics.description: An occupation is an organizing principle for information and ideas; it provides an axis that causes different experiences and facts to fall into order and hold relevant information because it is tied to needs and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure instruction around meaningful occupational problems or projects so knowledge is knitted under stress of practical use rather than abstract formal classification. Evaluate learning by its functional integration into occupational contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for occupations must be through occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: The only adequate training for occupations is training through occupations: engaging in active occupations indicated by the pupil's needs and interests, rather than predetermining narrow, direct vocational drills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor experiential, project-based, and apprenticeship-like approaches that let learners discover aptitudes and build occupation-related capacities. Anti-pattern: direct, early, rigid vocational specialization that sacrifices exploratory growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocational guidance should be ongoing and flexible
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of capacity and aptitude is a continuous process; conception of vocational guidance as leading to a definitive, irretrievable choice is injurious and tends to fossilize both education and vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide continual opportunities to explore and reorganize aims and methods across the life course; treat early vocational choices as provisional sketches rather than final determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocational education fosters active, purposeful learning
rubrics_metrics.description: An occupation is a continuous activity having a purpose; education through occupations appeals to instincts and habits, is a foe to passive receptivity, demands observation and ingenuity, and thus fulfills requirements for interest and thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design vocational tasks that have clear purposes and progressive stages requiring problem-solving, observation, and ingenuity. Use these tasks to promote sustained intellectual engagement rather than rote task completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic societies should allow intellectual freedom and play of diverse gifts
rubrics_metrics.description: A democratic society must, in consistency with its ideal, allow for intellectual freedom and the play of diverse gifts and interests in its educational measures; society counts individual variations as precious means of its own growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align educational policy and practice with democratic aims by protecting intellectual freedom, promoting diversity of talents, and resisting education that confines individuals to class-based or traditional roles.
